title: The Bravyi–König bound for topological Pauli stabilizer codes
markdown:
# The Bravyi–König bound for topological Pauli stabilizer codes

> Level 2 derivation: why a geometrically local, bounded-spread logical
> unitary on a \(D\)-dimensional topological Pauli stabilizer code cannot rise
> above level \(D\) of the Clifford hierarchy.

The memorable slogan is:

> **A constant-depth local circuit gets one hierarchy level per spatial
> dimension.**

The proof is not a statement about the surface code's particular square
lattice. It uses four ingredients that survive every change of stabilizer
layout:

1. local circuits have bounded light cones;
2. logical Paulis can be cleaned out of correctable regions;
3. a \(D\)-dimensional lattice can be partitioned into \(D+1\) correctable
   regions;
4. each group commutator removes one region from the possible support.

After \(D\) commutators, the remaining operator is trapped in the last
correctable region and therefore acts as a phase on the codespace. Reading
that statement backward is exactly the recursive definition of the Clifford
hierarchy.

## 1. Precise statement

Put physical qubits on a \(D\)-dimensional lattice. Let a **Pauli stabilizer
code** have

- stabilizer generators of geometric diameter at most \(\xi\);
- distance \(d\);
- a unitary \(U\), built from a depth-\(h\) circuit whose gates have geometric
  range at most \(r\);
- and the property that \(U\) preserves the codespace.

Write \(\overline U\) for the induced logical unitary. If \(D\geq 2\) and the
length scales obey

\[
        \xi,\;hr \ll d^{1/D},
\]

then

\[
        \overline U\in\mathcal C_D,
\]

where \(\mathcal C_D\) is level \(D\) of the Clifford hierarchy.

For a family with bounded \(\xi,h,r\) and growing distance, the scale
inequality holds for every sufficiently large member. “Constant depth” is
therefore the clean asymptotic formulation, but the actual resource in the
proof is the light-cone radius \(hr\).

The paper proves a stronger morphism version. The source and target may be two
different \(D\)-dimensional topological Pauli stabilizer codes on the same lattice,
with the same number of logical qubits. If \(U\) maps the first codespace
unitarily onto the second, use the smaller distance and the larger stabilizer
range in the scale inequality; the induced map is still in
\(\mathcal C_D\). The codespace-preserving theorem is the special case in
which the two codes coincide.

Immediate specializations:

- \(D=2\): \(\overline U\in\mathcal C_2\), the Clifford group. A logical
  \(T\) gate is excluded.
- \(D=3\): \(\overline U\in\mathcal C_3\). This level contains non-Clifford
  gates such as \(T\), so the theorem permits them but does not guarantee
  that a given code has one.

For the modern convention \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\),
\(TXT^\dagger=(X+Y)/\sqrt2\), which is a Clifford but not a Pauli, while
\(TZT^\dagger=Z\). Thus \(T\in\mathcal C_3\setminus\mathcal C_2\), making it
the simplest witness to the difference between the two- and
three-dimensional ceilings.

## 2. Dictionary

All Pauli phases are irrelevant below.

### 2.1 Stabilizers, logicals, and encoded action

Let \(\mathcal S\) be the stabilizer group and \(\Pi\) the codespace
projector. A physical Pauli \(P\) is a logical Pauli when it commutes with
every stabilizer. Two such Paulis have the same encoded action when they
differ by a stabilizer.

Choose an encoding isometry

\[
        J:(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes k}\longrightarrow
        (\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n},
        \qquad JJ^\dagger=\Pi .
\]

For a physical operator \(O\) preserving the codespace, its encoded action is

\[
        \overline O=J^\dagger OJ .
\]

The distance \(d\) is the minimum weight of a logical Pauli whose encoded
action is not a scalar.

The map from commuting physical Paulis to encoded Paulis has kernel exactly
\(\mathcal S\), up to phase. Suppose a Pauli \(P\) commutes with
\(\mathcal S\), fixes every code state, and is independent of
\(\mathcal S\). Adding \(P\) as a new independent stabilizer would halve the
joint \(+1\) eigenspace, yet by assumption it would leave that eigenspace
unchanged. The contradiction shows that \(P\) was already a stabilizer.

### 2.2 Correctable regions

A set of qubits \(M\) is **correctable** when every logical Pauli supported
entirely in \(M\) acts as a scalar on the codespace. Any set with fewer than
\(d\) qubits is correctable by the definition of distance.

Correctability is stronger than the Pauli-only wording suggests. If \(O\) is
any operator supported in \(M\), expand it in the Pauli basis:

\[
        O=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha P_\alpha .
\]

For each \(P_\alpha\):

- if it anticommutes with a stabilizer \(S\), then
  \(\Pi P_\alpha\Pi=\Pi SP_\alpha\Pi
  =-\Pi P_\alpha S\Pi=-\Pi P_\alpha\Pi=0\);
- if it commutes with every stabilizer, it is a logical Pauli in \(M\), so
  correctability gives
  \(\Pi P_\alpha\Pi=x_\alpha\Pi\).

Therefore

\[
        \Pi O\Pi=c(O)\Pi                                      \tag{2.1}
\]

for every operator supported in a correctable region. In particular, a
logical unitary supported there is logically only a phase.

### 2.3 Neighborhoods and circuit range

For a region \(M\), let \(B_\rho(M)\) contain all lattice sites within
distance \(\rho\) of \(M\). A depth-\(h\), range-\(r\) circuit expands support
by at most \(hr\):

\[
 \operatorname{supp}(UOU^\dagger)
 \subseteq B_{hr}(\operatorname{supp}O).                     \tag{2.2}
\]

This follows one layer at a time. In one layer, only gates meeting the current
support can matter, and each such gate reaches at most distance \(r\).

### 2.4 Clifford hierarchy

Let \(\mathcal C_1\) be the logical Pauli group. Recursively,

\[
 \mathcal C_j=
 \{V:VPV^\dagger\in\mathcal C_{j-1}
       \text{ for every logical Pauli }P\}.
                                                                  \tag{2.3}
\]

Thus \(\mathcal C_2\) is the Clifford group. The hierarchy is nested, but
\(\mathcal C_j\) is generally not a group for \(j\geq3\). Multiplying an
element of \(\mathcal C_j\) on either side by a Pauli leaves it in
\(\mathcal C_j\); this follows directly from (2.3), inducting on \(j\).

For unitaries \(A,B\), write their group commutator as

\[
        [A,B]=ABA^\dagger B^\dagger .
\]

The proof repeatedly asks what happens to the hierarchy level when such a
commutator becomes simpler.

## 3. Four lemmas

### 3.1 Cleaning Lemma

**Lemma.** If \(M\) is correctable, every logical Pauli \(P\) has an equivalent
representative with no support in \(M\).

**Proof.** Represent phase-free \(n\)-qubit Paulis by vectors in
\(\mathbb F_2^{2n}\), with the symplectic product recording commutation. Let
\(\mathsf S\) be the vector space spanned by the stabilizers, let
\(\mathsf S^\perp\) be its symplectic orthogonal, and let
\(\pi_M\) restrict a Pauli vector to \(M\).

A logical Pauli is a vector \(p\in\mathsf S^\perp\). We need to find
\(s\in\mathsf S\) with

\[
        \pi_M(p+s)=0,
\]

or equivalently \(\pi_M(p)\in\pi_M(\mathsf S)\).

Assume instead that \(\pi_M(p)\notin\pi_M(\mathsf S)\). The symplectic form on
the Pauli space of \(M\) is nondegenerate, so there is a Pauli vector \(q\)
supported in \(M\) such that

\[
 \langle q,\pi_M(s)\rangle=0
 \quad\text{for every }s\in\mathsf S,
 \qquad
 \langle q,\pi_M(p)\rangle=1 .
\]

Extended by zero outside \(M\), \(q\) commutes with every stabilizer and is
therefore a logical Pauli supported in \(M\). Correctability says its encoded
action is scalar, so \(q\) is a stabilizer up to phase. But \(p\), being
logical, must commute with every stabilizer, contradicting
\(\langle q,p\rangle=1\). Hence the required \(s\) exists. Multiplying \(P\)
by its stabilizer representative removes its support from \(M\) without
changing its encoded action. \(\square\)

Cleaning does not erase a logical operator. It moves the same logical class
out of a region known to contain no logical information.

### 3.2 Union Lemma

**Lemma.** Let \(M\) and \(N\) be correctable regions separated by more than
the maximum stabilizer-generator diameter \(\xi\). Then \(M\cup N\) is
correctable.

**Proof.** Let a logical Pauli \(P\) be supported in \(M\cup N\), and factor it
as \(P=P_M P_N\). No stabilizer generator can meet both regions. For a
generator meeting only \(M\), commutation with \(P\) is exactly commutation
with \(P_M\); similarly for \(N\). Because \(P\) commutes with every
generator, both \(P_M\) and \(P_N\) commute with every generator separately.
They are logical Paulis supported in correctable regions, so both have scalar
encoded action. Their product does too. \(\square\)

Induction gives the version used below: a union of mutually well-separated
correctable chunks is correctable. This is the first indispensable use of
stabilizer locality. Without local generators, one generator could touch two
distant chunks and the factorization argument would fail.

### 3.3 Causal-intersection Lemma

**Lemma.** Let \(P,Q\) be tensor-product Paulis and let \(U\) be a
depth-\(h\), range-\(r\) circuit. Up to a constant factor in the radius, the
commutator

\[
        K=[P,UQU^\dagger]
\]

can have support only where the causal neighborhoods of
\(\operatorname{supp}P\) and \(\operatorname{supp}Q\) meet.

**Proof.** Draw the circuit for \(UQU^\dagger\). Delete every gate of \(U\)
and \(U^\dagger\) outside the forward and backward light cones of
\(\operatorname{supp}Q\). Those gates occur in mutually inverse pairs and
cancel, so this deletion does not change \(UQU^\dagger\).

Now place this pruned circuit next to its inverse in
\(P(UQU^\dagger)P^\dagger(UQ^\dagger U^\dagger)\). Delete every remaining
gate whose causal cone misses \(\operatorname{supp}P\). It also meets its
inverse without encountering \(P\), so it cancels. What survives must lie
both near \(\operatorname{supp}Q\) and near
\(\operatorname{supp}P\). The composite circuit has depth \(O(h)\), so the
thickening radius is \(O(hr)\). \(\square\)

This is the second indispensable use of locality. A long-range gate can join
the two supports without passing through their geometric intersection.

### 3.4 Pauli-character Lemma

**Lemma.** Let \(V\) be a logical unitary. If

\[
        [P,V]\propto I
\]

for every logical Pauli \(P\), then \(V\) is a logical Pauli up to phase.

**Proof.** The assumption is equivalent to

\[
        PVP^\dagger=\chi(P)V .
\]

Conjugating twice by the same Pauli gives \(\chi(P)^2=1\), so every
\(\chi(P)\) is a commutation sign. Expand \(V\) in the logical Pauli basis.
Every nonzero Pauli component must have the same commutation sign
\(\chi(P)\) against every \(P\). Two distinct Paulis cannot have identical
commutation signs against the entire Pauli group: their product would be a
nonidentity Pauli commuting with every Pauli, contradicting nondegeneracy of
the symplectic form. Only one Pauli coefficient can therefore be nonzero.
\(\square\)

## 4. The geometric partition

Choose a mesoscopic length \(R\) satisfying

\[
        \max(\xi,c_Dhr)\ll R\ll d_*^{1/D},                    \tag{4.1}
\]

where \(d_*\) is the smaller source/target distance and \(c_D\) is a constant
large enough to contain every light cone created by the \(D\) nested
commutators below.

Triangulate the physical lattice at scale \(R\). Thicken the simplices in
order of dimension:

- \(\Lambda_1\) is a union of separated neighborhoods of vertices;
- \(\Lambda_2\) is a union of separated interiors of edges after the vertex
  neighborhoods are removed;
- continue through faces and higher-dimensional simplices;
- \(\Lambda_{D+1}\) is the union of the remaining interiors of the
  \(D\)-simplices.

These \(D+1\) regions partition the lattice. Each \(\Lambda_j\) is a union of
chunks with diameter \(O(R)\), while distinct chunks in the same region are
separated by \(\Omega(R)\).

A fixed-radius neighborhood of one chunk contains \(O(R^D)\) qubits. The
right inequality in (4.1) makes this number smaller than \(d_*\), so the
chunk and every light-cone neighborhood needed below are correctable for
both codes. The left inequality keeps distinct thickened chunks farther apart
than the stabilizer range. The Union Lemma then makes each complete
\(\Lambda_j\), with the required collars, correctable.

### The two-dimensional picture

For \(D=2\), triangulate the surface into triangles of side \(R\):

- \(C\): disks around the vertices;
- \(B\): thickened edge segments after removing those disks;
- \(A\): the capped triangle interiors left over.

Each letter denotes many disconnected pieces, but pieces bearing the same
letter are far apart. Each letter is therefore one correctable region by the
Union Lemma.

On the toric or surface code, one can instead picture a horizontal logical
string and a displaced vertical logical string. After conjugation by a local
circuit, a string becomes a fat string; its commutator with the transverse
string lives near their small intersection. This is the right intuition.
It is not the general proof: an arbitrary two-dimensional stabilizer code
need not present every logical as a simple string. The \(A,B,C\) partition
plus cleaning supplies the same “small intersection” conclusion without
assuming string-shaped logicals.

## 5. Complete proof in two dimensions

Use the stronger two-code formulation. Let \(\Pi_1,\Pi_2\) project onto the
source and target codespaces, and suppose

\[
        U\Pi_1U^\dagger=\Pi_2 .
\]

Choose the partition \(\Lambda=A\cup B\cup C\) above, with collars wide enough
for all circuit light cones.

Let \(Q\) be an arbitrary logical Pauli of the source code and \(P\) an
arbitrary logical Pauli of the target code.

1. Since \(B_\rho(A)\) is correctable for the source code, clean \(Q\) out of
   \(B_\rho(A)\).
2. Since \(B_\rho(B)\) is correctable for the target code, clean \(P\) out of
   \(B_\rho(B)\).
3. Form the target-code logical operator

   \[
        K=P(UQU^\dagger)P^\dagger(UQ^\dagger U^\dagger).
                                                                  \tag{5.1}
   \]

The cleaned \(Q\) has no support near \(A\), so the bounded light cone of
\(UQU^\dagger\) avoids \(A\). The cleaned \(P\) has no support near \(B\).
By the Causal-intersection Lemma, all parts of (5.1) away from the common
causal intersection cancel. Thus \(K\) is supported in \(C\).

Every factor in (5.1) preserves the target codespace: \(P\) is a target
logical, while \(UQU^\dagger\) is the image of a source logical under the
codespace morphism. Hence \(K\) is a logical unitary supported in the
correctable region \(C\). Equation (2.1) gives

\[
        K\Pi_2=c\Pi_2,\qquad |c|=1.                              \tag{5.2}
\]

In fact \(c=\pm1\). On the codespace let
\(R=\overline U\,\overline Q\,\overline U^\dagger\). Equation (5.2) says

\[
        \overline P R\overline P^\dagger R^\dagger=cI,
        \quad\text{or}\quad
        \overline P R\overline P^\dagger=cR .
\]

Conjugating a second time by the Pauli \(\overline P\) yields
\(R=c^2R\), so \(c^2=1\).

We have proved

\[
        [\overline P,
          \overline U\,\overline Q\,\overline U^\dagger]
        =\pm I                                                    \tag{5.3}
\]

for every target Pauli \(\overline P\) and every source Pauli
\(\overline Q\). Fixing \(Q\), the Pauli-character Lemma turns (5.3) into

\[
        \overline U\,\overline Q\,\overline U^\dagger
        \in\mathcal C_1 .
\]

This is true for every \(\overline Q\), which is precisely the definition

\[
        \overline U\in\mathcal C_2 .
\]

So every such two-dimensional logical unitary is Clifford. No translation
symmetry, square lattice, homological presentation, or string form for the
logical operators entered the proof.

## 6. The \(D\)-dimensional induction

Partition the lattice into the \(D+1\) correctable regions

\[
        \Lambda=\Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup\Lambda_{D+1}.
\]

Choose an arbitrary source logical Pauli \(P_1\), and arbitrary target
logical Paulis \(P_2,\ldots,P_D\). Use the Cleaning Lemma to choose
representatives satisfying

\[
 \operatorname{supp}(P_j)\cap B_\rho(\Lambda_j)=\varnothing,
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,D.                                           \tag{6.1}
\]

Define

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 K_1 &= UP_1U^\dagger,\\
 K_j &=P_j^\dagger K_{j-1}P_jK_{j-1}^\dagger,
        \qquad j=2,\ldots,D .                                   \tag{6.2}
 \end{aligned}
\]

Every \(K_j\) preserves the target codespace. We now track support.

- Because \(P_1\) was cleaned out of a collar of \(\Lambda_1\), causal
  pruning of the circuit \(UP_1U^\dagger\) gives a representation of \(K_1\)
  acting trivially on \(\Lambda_1\).
- Suppose \(K_{j-1}\) acts trivially on
  \(\Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup\Lambda_{j-1}\). The next line of (6.2) is its
  commutator with \(P_j\). Since \(P_j\) was cleaned out of a collar of
  \(\Lambda_j\), the Causal-intersection Lemma removes \(\Lambda_j\) from the
  support as well. The already removed regions stay removed because their
  collars were chosen wider than the new constant-depth light cone.

The depth of these nested commutator circuits grows by only a
\(D\)-dependent constant factor. That is why one common radius
\(\rho=c_Dhr\) suffices in (4.1). Induction gives

\[
 \operatorname{supp}(K_j)
 \subseteq
 \Lambda_{j+1}\cup\cdots\cup\Lambda_{D+1}.                       \tag{6.3}
\]

At \(j=D\), \(K_D\) is a logical unitary supported in the correctable region
\(\Lambda_{D+1}\). Therefore

\[
        \overline K_D\propto I                                   \tag{6.4}
\]

for every choice of \(P_1,\ldots,P_D\).

Now read the nested commutators backward.

First, (6.2) and (6.4) say that

\[
        [\overline P_D,\overline K_{D-1}]\propto I
\]

for every Pauli \(\overline P_D\). The Pauli-character Lemma gives

\[
        \overline K_{D-1}\in\mathcal C_1 .
\]

For the induction step, suppose
\(\overline K_j\in\mathcal C_m\) for every choice of
\(\overline P_j\). Rearranging (6.2) gives

\[
 \overline K_{j-1}\overline P_j\overline K_{j-1}^\dagger
     =\overline P_j\,\overline K_j .                             \tag{6.5}
\]

The right-hand side belongs to \(\mathcal C_m\), because multiplying by a
Pauli preserves a hierarchy level. Since (6.5) holds for every Pauli
\(\overline P_j\), definition (2.3) gives

\[
        \overline K_{j-1}\in\mathcal C_{m+1}.
\]

Repeating this backward yields

\[
        \overline K_1\in\mathcal C_{D-1}.
\]

Finally \(K_1=UP_1U^\dagger\), and \(P_1\) was an arbitrary source logical
Pauli. Hence

\[
        \boxed{\overline U\in\mathcal C_D}.
\]

The dimension enters only through the number of correctable regions. Each
commutator consumes one region, so \(D\) spatial dimensions leave exactly
\(D\) hierarchy levels.

## 7. Why the result also forbids a protected universal gate set

For a fixed number \(k\) of logical qubits, every finite level
\(\mathcal C_j\) contains only finitely many elements up to global phase.
This can be proved recursively. The Pauli group is finite up to phase. An
element of \(\mathcal C_j\) is specified, up to phase, by its conjugation
action on a finite generating set of Paulis, and every image lies in the
finite set \(\mathcal C_{j-1}\). If two unitaries have the same conjugation
action on every Pauli, their ratio commutes with the full matrix algebra and
is a scalar.

There is one subtlety: \(\mathcal C_D\) is not generally a group when
\(D\geq3\), so “every generator lies in \(\mathcal C_D\)” does not alone show
that all generated products remain there.

The depth assumption closes this loophole. If a product of protected
depth-\(h\) gates first left \(\mathcal C_D\) after a bounded number \(s\) of
factors, that product would itself have depth \(sh=O(1)\). The theorem would
put it back in \(\mathcal C_D\), a contradiction. Because
\(\mathcal C_D\) is finite for fixed \(k\), the maximum possible shortest
escape length over its subsets is finite. Thus, for all sufficiently large
codes, the group generated by bounded-depth protected gates remains inside a
finite set and cannot be computationally universal.

The fixed-\(k\) qualification belongs to this universality corollary. The
main hierarchy bound itself is the local statement proved in Sections 4–6.

## 8. What is and is not an escape

| Proposed maneuver | Does the theorem apply? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Change the shape or tiling of a 2D stabilizer code | Yes, if locality and macroscopic distance remain | The proof never uses a square lattice or translation symmetry |
| Use a geometrically local transversal physical gate | Yes | It is a particularly shallow local circuit; transversality alone does not make distant pairings geometrically local |
| Use a bounded-depth local unitary deformation between two codes | Yes | The morphism version allows distinct source and target codes |
| Braid defects through a chain of uniformly local 2D deformations | Still Clifford | Each protected local step is Clifford, and the Clifford group is closed |
| Use lattice surgery with depth growing with code distance | Not as one constant-depth unitary | Its growing time depth lies outside the theorem's circuit assumption; its standard logical operations are nevertheless Clifford |
| Inject and distill magic states | Injection is outside the protected hypothesis | At injection, the new logical state does not yet have macroscopic topological protection |
| Use measurements and adaptive classical feedback | Not covered by the literal unitary-circuit statement | A separate analysis is needed for nonunitary protocols |
| Couple distant planar qubits directly | No | The gate range is no longer geometrically bounded in the planar metric |
| Let circuit depth grow until \(hr\) is comparable to \(d^{1/D}\) | No | The mesoscopic scale \(R\) in (4.1) no longer exists |
| Replace commuting Pauli checks by generalized non-Pauli stabilizers | No | The Pauli symplectic Cleaning and Union Lemmas used here no longer apply |
| Move from 2D to 3D | Yes, with a weaker ceiling | The allowed level rises from \(\mathcal C_2\) to \(\mathcal C_3\) |

The theorem is a ceiling, not a construction. It says which hierarchy levels
are impossible under its assumptions; it does not say that every gate below
the ceiling is available for every code.

### A current boundary case: “Clifford stabilizer codes”

Kobayashi, Zhu, and Hsin constructed a two-dimensional code with a
transversal logical \(T\) gate in 2026 and explicitly described it as
surpassing the Bravyi–König bound for **Pauli** codes. There is no
contradiction. Their local “stabilizers” are Clifford unitaries rather than
Pauli operators and need not commute. The object is therefore outside the
abelian Pauli stabilizer formalism assumed in Sections 1–6.

This distinction is load-bearing, not terminological. The proof of the
Cleaning Lemma used the symplectic vector space of Pauli operators; the Union
Lemma factorized commutation with bounded-diameter Pauli generators; and
equation (2.1) expanded errors in the Pauli basis relative to an abelian
Pauli stabilizer codespace. Those steps cannot simply be reused for
noncommuting Clifford generators. The 2026 construction changes the
algebraic hypothesis that makes the Bravyi–König ceiling possible.

## 9. Audit questions

**Q1. Why is the scale \(d^{1/D}\), rather than \(d\)?**

**A.** A chunk of linear size \(R\) in \(D\) dimensions contains
\(O(R^D)\) qubits. Distance guarantees correctability when that volume is
smaller than \(d\), hence \(R\ll d^{1/D}\).

**Q2. Where exactly is stabilizer locality used?**

**A.** In the Union Lemma. Widely separated correctable chunks remain
correctable because no bounded-diameter stabilizer generator can couple two
chunks. Circuit locality is a separate use of geometry: it bounds light
cones in the Causal-intersection Lemma.

**Q3. Why may a non-Pauli commutator \(K_D\) be declared trivial in a
correctable region?**

**A.** Correctability plus Pauli expansion gives
\(\Pi O\Pi=c(O)\Pi\) for every operator \(O\) in the region, not only for
Paulis. Since \(K_D\) also preserves the codespace, its logical action is
that scalar.

**Q4. Why is the crossing-string argument insufficient as the general
proof?**

**A.** It presumes convenient string representatives. The theorem covers
arbitrary local stabilizer codes. The simplicial partition and Cleaning
Lemma manufacture the needed separated supports without assuming any
particular shape for a logical operator.

**Q5. Does the 3D conclusion provide a universal protected gate set?**

**A.** No. It permits level-3 gates such as \(T\), but for fixed \(k\) the
bounded-depth protected gates still generate only a finite subgroup inside
the hierarchy ceiling. Additional unprotected or nonunitary resources remain
necessary for universality.

## 10. Source and citation audit

Primary source, fetch-verified on 2026-07-26:

- Sergey Bravyi and Robert König, “Classification of topologically protected
  gates for local stabilizer codes,”
  [arXiv:1206.1609](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.1609), submitted 7 June 2012;
  [Physical Review Letters 110, 170503
  (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.110.170503).

Scope-boundary source, also fetch-verified on 2026-07-26:

- Ryohei Kobayashi, Guanyu Zhu, and Po-Shen Hsin, “Clifford Hierarchy
  Stabilizer Codes: Transversal Non-Clifford Gates and Magic,”
  [arXiv:2511.02900](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02900);
  journal version, “Clifford Hierarchy Stabilizer Codes: Transversal
  Non-Clifford Gates and Magic States,”
  [Physical Review Letters 136, 250802
  (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1103/j2q4-bnc6).

The theorem statement, the scale condition, the two-code morphism
generalization, the Cleaning and Union Lemmas, the simplicial partition, the
nested-commutator proof, and the fixed-\(k\) universality corollary all trace
to this source. The intermediate symplectic proof of cleaning, the
Pauli-basis proof of (2.1), and the expanded hierarchy induction are supplied
here so that the paper is provenance rather than a missing proof step.

Atlas citation note: `atlas/surface/card.yaml` currently uses the bibkey
`bravyi2013classification`, while
`docs/lit/surface/surface-foundations.md` uses
`bravyikonig2013classification` for the same fetch-verified paper. T4 permits
new files only, so this page records the mismatch instead of changing either
out-of-scope file. The planned reference-registry task should choose one key
and enforce it repository-wide.

title: The Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal tradeoff in two dimensions
markdown:
# The Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal tradeoff in two dimensions

> Level 2 derivation: why bounded-range commuting constraints in an ordinary
> two-dimensional geometry force \(k d^2=O(n)\).

The memorable slogan is:

> **In two Euclidean dimensions, one distance-\(d\) logical qubit consumes
> area of order \(d^2\).**

This is not proved by drawing a logical string and counting its length. A
general commuting-projector code need not be a stabilizer code and need not
have string-shaped logical operators. The proof instead turns local
correctability into an entropy statement:

1. a correctable square can be enlarged whenever its boundary is also
   correctable;
2. therefore every square whose side is a sufficiently small constant
   multiple of \(d\) is correctable;
3. the lattice can be divided into two correctable checkerboards \(A,B\)
   plus small corner patches \(C\);
4. correctability of \(A\) and \(B\) forces all \(k\) logical qubits through
   \(C\);
5. the area of \(C\) is \(O(n/d^2)\).

The third step is where two-dimensional geometry enters. The fourth is
where quantum information differs from classical information: a region
whose erasure is correctable has *negative* conditional entropy.

## 1. Precise statement

Put \(n\) particles on a regular square lattice with open or periodic
boundary conditions. Assume:

- every site has Hilbert-space dimension at most a fixed \(q\);
- the codespace \(\mathcal C\) is the common \(+1\) eigenspace of pairwise
  commuting projectors \(\Pi_a\);
- the support of every \(\Pi_a\) fits inside a \(w\times w\) square;
- \(\dim\mathcal C=2^k\);
- every erasure on fewer than \(d\) sites is correctable.

Here \(w\) and \(q\) are independent of the lattice size. Then there is a
constant \(c(w,q)\), independent of \(n,k,d\), such that

\[
             \boxed{k\,d^2\leq c(w,q)\,n.}                     \tag{1.1}
\]

The theorem is often called a stabilizer-code bound because stabilizer
codes are its most common application. The original result is stronger:
commuting local projectors need not be Pauli projectors.

Three qualifications are load-bearing.

1. **Local means Euclidean bounded range.** A weight-six check may still be
   nonlocal if its six qubits separate by a distance growing with the code.
2. **The constraints commute.** The boundary factorization below uses
   commutativity, not merely a gapped local Hamiltonian.
3. **The local dimension is bounded.** Otherwise one site can hide a growing
   number of qubits and the entropy count \(S(C)\leq |C|\log_2q\) has no
   size-independent coefficient.

If \(k=0\), (1.1) is immediate. The proof below therefore assumes \(k>0\).
Cases with \(d\) comparable to the fixed microscopic scale \(w^2\) are also
immediate from \(k\leq n\log_2q\); the geometric argument handles the
macroscopic-distance regime.

## 2. Dictionary: what “correctable” means

Let

\[
       \Pi=\prod_a\Pi_a
\]

be the codespace projector. For a set of sites \(M\), write
\(\overline M\) for its complement.

### 2.1 Erasure criterion

A region \(M\) is **correctable** when erasing all sites in \(M\) can be
reversed on every encoded state. The Knill–Laflamme condition for this
known-location error is

\[
        \Pi O_M\Pi=c(O_M)\Pi
        \quad\text{for every operator }O_M
        \text{ supported in }M.                               \tag{2.1}
\]

Why does (2.1) characterize erasure? Choose an operator basis
\(\{E_\alpha\}\) on \(M\). Erasure has error products
\(E_\alpha^\dagger E_\beta\), and these span the full operator algebra on
\(M\). The ordinary Knill–Laflamme equations for all pairs
\(\alpha,\beta\) are therefore exactly (2.1).

Two consequences will be used repeatedly.

- Any subset of a correctable region is correctable.
- Every region with fewer than \(d\) sites is correctable, by the definition
  of distance used in the theorem.

For a Pauli stabilizer code, (2.1) says that a region contains no
nontrivial logical Pauli. Thus this erasure distance agrees with the usual
minimum weight of a nontrivial logical Pauli.

### 2.2 The entropy identity

Let \(\rho\) be any encoded state. Correctability of \(M\) implies

\[
          S(M\mid\overline M)=-S(M),                           \tag{2.2}
\]

where logarithms are base two.

Here is the information-theoretic content of the equation. Purify the
logical input with a reference \(R\), encode it into
\(M\overline M\), and apply (2.1). No observable on \(M\) depends on the
logical input, including its off-diagonal coherences, so

\[
          \rho_{RM}=\rho_R\otimes\rho_M .
\]

Equivalently \(I(R:M)=0\). The global state on
\(RM\overline M\) is pure, hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
0=I(R:M)
 &=S(R)+S(M)-S(RM)\\
 &=S(M\overline M)+S(M)-S(\overline M).
\end{aligned}
\]

Rearranging gives (2.2). The negative sign is not a formal curiosity:
\(\overline M\) can reconstruct the quantum information lost from \(M\),
so the two regions share the entanglement needed to undo that loss.

For the maximally mixed encoded state

\[
             \rho_*=\frac{\Pi}{2^k},
\]

the entropy of the full lattice is

\[
             S(\Lambda)=k.                                    \tag{2.3}
\]

Equations (2.2) and (2.3) will convert geometry into a bound on \(k\).

### 2.3 Internal and external boundaries

The external boundary \(\partial_+M\subseteq\overline M\) contains every
outside site belonging to a projector that also touches \(M\). The internal
boundary is

\[
             \partial_-M=\partial_+(\overline M),
\]

and \(\partial M=\partial_-M\cup\partial_+M\).

For an \(R\times R\) square on a square lattice,

\[
             |\partial M|\leq c_\square\,w(R+w),               \tag{2.4}
\]

where \(c_\square\) is a geometry-only constant. Equation (2.4) is simply a
perimeter count: only a collar of thickness \(O(w)\) can participate in a
constraint crossing the cut.

## 3. Why commuting projectors can be split at a boundary

The proof must do more than clean Pauli operators. It must disentangle an
arbitrary commuting-projector codespace at the boundary of a correctable
region.

### 3.1 Boundary-algebra decomposition

Suppose two commuting projectors act on \(AB\) and \(BC\):

\[
        P_{AB}Q_{BC}=Q_{BC}P_{AB}.
\]

There is a decomposition

\[
 \mathcal H_B=
 \bigoplus_x
 \mathcal H_{B_x^L}\otimes\mathcal H_{B_x^R}                  \tag{3.1}
\]

such that, in every sector \(x\), the \(AB\) projector acts only on
\(AB_x^L\) and the \(BC\) projector acts only on \(B_x^RC\).

To see the mechanism, take operator-Schmidt expansions

\[
 P_{AB}=\sum_i A_i\otimes L_i,\qquad
 Q_{BC}=\sum_j R_j\otimes C_j
\]

with linearly independent outer operators. Commutativity forces
\([L_i,R_j]=0\) for every \(i,j\). The finite-dimensional algebras
\(\mathcal L=\operatorname{alg}\{L_i\}\) and
\(\mathcal R=\operatorname{alg}\{R_j\}\) therefore commute.

Decompose the center of \(\mathcal L\) into minimal central projectors.
Inside one central block, a finite-dimensional factor is a full matrix
algebra on one tensor factor with an identity on its multiplicity factor:

\[
       \mathcal L_x\simeq
       \mathsf M(\mathcal H_{B_x^L})\otimes I_{B_x^R}.
\]

Every operator commuting with \(\mathcal L_x\) acts on the other factor, so

\[
       \mathcal R_x\subseteq
       I_{B_x^L}\otimes\mathsf M(\mathcal H_{B_x^R}).
\]

This proves (3.1). The label \(x\) is a classical boundary sector; the left
and right quantum degrees of freedom separate inside each sector.

For many commuting constraints, group the product of all constraints
meeting the left side into \(P_{AB}\) and the product of the rest into
\(Q_{BC}\). Their interaction algebras obey the same decomposition.

### 3.2 Boundary Disentangling Lemma

**Lemma.** Let \(M\) and its external boundary \(\partial_+M\) both be
correctable. Then a unitary supported on \(\partial M\) transforms the
codespace projector into

\[
 U_{\partial M}\Pi U_{\partial M}^\dagger
       =|\phi_M\rangle\langle\phi_M|\otimes\Pi_{\overline M}
                                                               \tag{3.2}
\]

for a fixed pure state \(|\phi_M\rangle\) independent of the encoded state.

**Proof.** Partition the lattice as

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=M\setminus\partial_-M,& B&=\partial_-M,\\
C&=\partial_+M,& D&=\overline M\setminus\partial_+M.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(M=AB\), \(\overline M=CD\), and all communication between the two
interiors passes through \(BC\).

First split \(C\). Group the commuting constraints into those supported on
\(ABC\) and those supported on \(CD\). Applying (3.1) to their interaction
algebras gives

\[
 \Pi=\bigoplus_x
       \Pi^{(x)}_{AB\,C_x^L}\otimes
       \Pi^{(x)}_{C_x^R D}.                                   \tag{3.3}
\]

If two nonzero sectors \(x\) occurred, measuring the sector label on \(C\)
would distinguish orthogonal code states. That contradicts correctability
of \(C\subseteq\partial_+M\). Hence only one sector occurs, and a unitary
\(U_C\) exposes a tensor split \(C=C^LC^R\).

Apply the same argument to the internal boundary \(B\), grouping constraints
on \(AB\) against those on \(BCD\). Because \(B\subseteq M\) is correctable,
only one boundary sector occurs. After a unitary \(U_B\), the projector has
the product form

\[
 \Pi'=
     \Pi_{AB^L}\otimes
     \Theta_{B^R C^L}\otimes
     \Pi_{C^R D}.                                              \tag{3.4}
\]

Correctability of \(M\) forces \(\Pi_{AB^L}\) to have rank one. Otherwise
two orthogonal states in that factor could be distinguished by an
observable supported in \(M\).

The middle projector \(\Theta_{B^RC^L}\) also has rank one. If it encoded a
nontrivial system, correctability of \(B^R\subseteq M\) would make that
system recoverable from \(C^L\), while correctability of
\(C^L\subseteq\partial_+M\) would make the same system recoverable from
\(B^R\). Two disjoint systems would then each contain the full unknown
quantum state, contradicting no-cloning.

A final unitary on \(B^RC^L\) maps its fixed pure state into the \(M\)
factor. Together with \(U_B\) and \(U_C\), it gives (3.2). \(\square\)

The unitary \(U_{\partial M}\) need not be a geometrically local circuit
inside the boundary. The theorem needs only its support, not a depth bound.

### 3.3 Growth Lemma: a correctable boundary lets a region expand

**Lemma.** Write the lattice as \(ABCD\), with \(M=AB\). Suppose:

- \(M\) is correctable;
- \(BC\) is correctable;
- every constraint crossing the boundary of \(M\) is supported in \(BC\).

Then \(ABC=M\cup C\) is correctable.

**Proof.** Since \(\partial_+M\subseteq C\subseteq BC\), both \(M\) and its
external boundary are correctable. Apply (3.2). After the boundary unitary,
every encoded state has the form

\[
       \eta_{AB}\otimes\eta_{CD},                              \tag{3.5}
\]

where \(\eta_{AB}\) is a known pure state independent of the logical input.

Consider the error that first applies the boundary unitary from (3.2) and
then erases \(BC\). Its support lies in the correctable region \(BC\), so it has a
recovery map. Its surviving state is

\[
       \eta_A\otimes\rho_D.                                    \tag{3.6}
\]

The factor \(\eta_A\) is fixed and can be prepared for free. Therefore
\(\rho_D\) alone determines and reconstructs the original encoded state.
Erasure of \(ABC\) is correctable. \(\square\)

This is the holographic step: once the interior is known to be
correctable, only a boundary collar can obstruct enlarging it.

### 3.4 Separated-Union Lemma

**Lemma.** Let \(M_1,\ldots,M_t\) be correctable regions such that no local
projector overlaps two of them. If every external boundary
\(\partial_+M_i\) is correctable, then

\[
               M_1\cup\cdots\cup M_t
\]

is correctable.

**Proof.** It is enough to verify (2.1). Expand an arbitrary operator on the
union as a sum of tensor products
\(O_{M_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes O_{M_t}\).

Apply the factorization from the proof of the Disentangling Lemma to
\(M_1\). No constraint touching \(M_1\) reaches any other \(M_j\), so

\[
\Pi
 (O_{M_1}\otimes O_{M_2}\otimes\cdots\otimes O_{M_t})
\Pi
=f_1(O_{M_1})
\Pi(O_{M_2}\otimes\cdots\otimes O_{M_t})\Pi.                  \tag{3.7}
\]

Repeat for \(M_2,\ldots,M_t\). The result is

\[
       \Pi O\Pi=c(O)\Pi,
\]

which is (2.1) for the union. \(\square\)

This is the first point where bounded interaction range matters. Weight
alone is insufficient: one bounded-weight projector could touch two
distant blocks and prevent (3.7).

## 4. Holographic correctability: side length is linear in distance

Let \(R_*\) be the largest integer such that **every** \(R_*\times R_*\)
square is correctable. Such a maximum exists for \(k>0\), because the full
lattice cannot be erased and recovered.

Distance alone gives only \(R_*=\Omega(\sqrt d)\): a square with fewer than
\(d\) sites is correctable. Locality improves this to

\[
                    R_*=\Omega(d/w).                           \tag{4.1}
\]

Take any correctable \(R_*\times R_*\) square \(M\). Let \(B\) be an
internal collar and \(C\) an external collar, each of thickness sufficient
to contain the support of every constraint crossing the cut. Then
\(\partial M\subseteq BC\), and (2.4) gives

\[
                    |BC|\leq c_\square w(R_*+w).               \tag{4.2}
\]

Suppose the right-hand side were smaller than \(d\). The collar \(BC\)
would be correctable. The Growth Lemma would make \(M\cup C\), a strictly
larger square, correctable. The construction works at every position, so it
would contradict maximality of \(R_*\).

Therefore

\[
             d\leq c_\square w(R_*+w).                         \tag{4.3}
\]

When \(d\) is larger than a fixed multiple of \(w^2\), (4.3) gives (4.1).
When it is not, the final theorem follows from the trivial entropy bound
\(k\leq n\log_2q\) after enlarging \(c(w,q)\).

Now choose a smaller mesoscopic length

\[
             \ell=\left\lfloor\alpha\,\frac d w\right\rfloor, \tag{4.4}
\]

where the geometry-only constant \(\alpha>0\) is small enough that:

1. \(\ell\leq R_*\), so every \(\ell\times\ell\) square is correctable;
2. every width-\(O(w)\) boundary collar of such a square has fewer than
   \(d\) sites and is therefore correctable.

This is the exact content hidden by the phrase “a box of side proportional
to \(d\) is correctable.” The proportionality constant depends on the
interaction range because the information bottleneck is the perimeter
\(O(w\ell)\).

## 5. The checkerboard partition

Tile the lattice by \(\ell\times\ell\) squares and color the tiles black and
white in a checkerboard pattern.

- \(A\) is the union of the black tiles after shaving an \(O(w)\)-sized
  patch from every corner.
- \(B\) is the analogous union of the white tiles.
- \(C\) is the union of all shaved corner patches.

The corner patches have two jobs. Black tiles meet other black tiles only
at corners, as do white tiles. Removing a collar wider than the interaction
range ensures that no projector touches two components of \(A\), and no
projector touches two components of \(B\).

Each component of \(A\) or \(B\) is a subset of an
\(\ell\times\ell\) correctable square. Its external boundary is correctable
by the choice of \(\ell\). The Separated-Union Lemma therefore gives:

\[
                        A\text{ and }B\text{ are correctable}. \tag{5.1}
\]

There are \(O(n/\ell^2)\) tile corners, and each removed patch contains
\(O(w^2)\) sites. Boundary fragments at the edge of an open lattice change
only the geometry constant. Hence

\[
                         |C|\leq c_C\,\frac{n w^2}{\ell^2}.     \tag{5.2}
\]

The diagram to keep in mind is not “large boxes separated by wide
corridors.” Wide corridors would occupy \(O(nw/\ell)\) sites and lose one
power of \(d\). The checkerboard needs only codimension-two intersections:
in two dimensions, those are isolated corner patches.

## 6. The entropy calculation

Evaluate the maximally mixed code state \(\rho_*=\Pi/2^k\) on the partition
\(\Lambda=ABC\).

Correctability of \(A\) and (2.2) give

\[
\begin{aligned}
k
  &=S(ABC)\\
  &=S(BC)+S(A\mid BC)\\
  &=S(BC)-S(A)\\
  &\leq S(B)+S(C)-S(A).                                      \tag{6.1}
\end{aligned}
\]

The last line is subadditivity. Interchanging \(A\) and \(B\) gives

\[
              k\leq S(A)+S(C)-S(B).                           \tag{6.2}
\]

Add (6.1) and (6.2). The unknown entropies of the two large checkerboards
cancel:

\[
                         k\leq S(C).                           \tag{6.3}
\]

Each site has dimension at most \(q\), so

\[
                         S(C)\leq |C|\log_2q.                  \tag{6.4}
\]

Substitute (5.2) and \(\ell=\Theta(d/w)\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
k
 &\leq c_C\log_2q\,\frac{n w^2}{\ell^2}\\
 &\leq c'(w,q)\,\frac{n}{d^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
                         \boxed{k d^2\leq c'(w,q)n}.
\]

That completes the proof.

The flow of logical information is now visible. Both extensive regions
\(A\) and \(B\) may be erased. Quantum information cannot reside in either
one, yet together they cover almost the whole lattice. Their two entropy
identities force the logical entropy into the sparse intersection skeleton
\(C\), and geometry makes that skeleton too small to carry more than
\(O(n/d^2)\) qubits.

## 7. Consequences and saturation

### 7.1 Fixed \(k\)

For any family encoding at least one logical qubit,

\[
                         d=O(\sqrt n).
\]

This is why a two-dimensional surface-code patch with
\(n=\Theta(d^2)\) has the optimal distance exponent. The theorem does not
select the surface code or its constant prefactor; it says no code under the
same hypotheses can improve the exponent.

### 7.2 Nonzero rate

If \(k/n\) stays above a positive constant, then

\[
                         d=O(1).
\]

Thus a two-dimensional bounded-range commuting-projector family cannot
simultaneously have constant rate and growing distance.

### 7.3 Tightness

One planar surface-code patch has

\[
             k=1,\qquad n=\Theta(d^2).
\]

Placing \(k\) independent patches side by side gives

\[
             n=\Theta(kd^2).
\]

The BPT scaling is therefore tight up to a constant depending on layout and
microscopic locality. Rotating a patch or changing its boundary convention
can improve that constant, but cannot change the exponent while the theorem's
hypotheses remain true.

### 7.4 Higher dimensions

The same proof in \(D\) Euclidean dimensions uses a codimension-two
skeleton:

- the sparse region has size \(O(n/\ell^2)\);
- a cube of side \(\ell\) has boundary size
  \(O(\ell^{D-1})\);
- holographic correctability permits
  \(\ell^{D-1}=O(d)\).

Consequently,

\[
                k\leq c_D\,\frac{n}{d^{\,2/(D-1)}}.            \tag{7.1}
\]

For \(D=2\), (7.1) is the bound proved above. The original paper explicitly
notes that its higher-dimensional exponent need not be tight.

### 7.5 Why the classical companion has a different exponent

The same paper proves that a two-dimensional classical code specified by
bounded-range constraints obeys

\[
                         k\sqrt d=O(n).                         \tag{7.2}
\]

The shorter proof exposes the quantum difference. Choose separated square
blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\), each containing fewer than \(d\) sites and having
side \(\Theta(\sqrt d)\). Let \(B=\bigcup_iB_i\), and let \(A\) be the
width-\(O(w)\) grid between them. Then

\[
                         |A|=O(nw/\sqrt d).                    \tag{7.3}
\]

Suppose two classical codewords \(x,y\) agree on \(A\). If they differ
inside some block \(B_i\), splice a new assignment \(z\): use \(x\) on
\(B_i\) and \(y\) everywhere else. Every local constraint sees at most one
block, and constraints meeting \(B_i\) see the same boundary values from
\(x\) and \(y\), so \(z\) is another codeword. But \(z\) and \(y\) differ
on fewer than \(d\) sites, contradicting distance. Therefore agreement on
\(A\) determines the whole codeword.

The restriction map from codewords to configurations on \(A\) is injective.
For bounded local alphabet size, the number of encoded bits satisfies

\[
                         k\leq c_q|A|,
\]

which together with (7.3) gives (7.2).

Classically, one thin grid is enough because a codeword can be copied and
compared. Quantumly, no-cloning and entanglement replace unique extension by
the negative conditional-entropy identity. Two correctable checkerboards are
needed, and their entropy cancellation leaves a codimension-two set. That is
why the quantum tradeoff contains \(d^2\), while the classical companion
contains only \(\sqrt d\).

## 8. What does and does not evade the theorem

| Change | Covered? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Replace square plaquettes by another bounded-density 2D tiling | Yes | Only bounded Euclidean geometry and bounded interaction range enter |
| Use qudits of a fixed dimension | Yes | The coefficient acquires a factor depending on \(\log_2 q\) |
| Use a Pauli stabilizer code with local generators | Yes | It is a special case of commuting local projectors |
| Keep checks low-weight but connect sites a growing Euclidean distance apart | No | Weight does not bound \(w\); the separated-union step fails |
| Embed the Tanner graph in two layers with long bridges | Not with a size-independent \(w\) | The relevant metric is the physical Euclidean layout, including bridges |
| Let the interaction range grow with \(n\) | No uniform asymptotic bound | The hidden coefficient depends on \(w\) |
| Use noncommuting local gauge checks of a subsystem code | Not by the original theorem | The commuting-projector boundary decomposition is unavailable |
| Move to a non-Euclidean family of graphs | Not as stated | The checkerboard and codimension-two counting use ordinary Euclidean growth |
| Move to \(D>2\) | A different tradeoff applies | Use (7.1), not the two-dimensional exponent |
| Improve a finite block's value of \(kd^2/n\) | Possibly | The theorem fixes asymptotic scaling, not a universal finite-size constant |

Two common confusions deserve emphasis.

**LDPC is not geometric locality.** LDPC bounds how many qubits a check
touches and how many checks touch a qubit. BPT additionally requires those
qubits to lie in a bounded Euclidean neighborhood. A family may be qLDPC
and still lie outside BPT.

**BPT is not a threshold theorem.** It constrains the static code parameters
\((n,k,d)\). It says nothing by itself about syndrome circuits, decoder
runtime, noise thresholds, or logical error rates.

## 9. BPT versus nearby no-go theorems

| Result | Resource constrained | Typical conclusion in 2D |
|---|---|---|
| Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal | Static information density under local commuting constraints | \(kd^2=O(n)\) |
| Bravyi–König | Logical gates implemented by bounded-depth local circuits | Only Clifford logical gates |
| Bravyi–Terhal | Thermal energy barrier of 2D local stabilizer Hamiltonians | No growing stabilizer energy barrier |
| Eastin–Knill | Exactly transversal gates on a finite-dimensional exact code | No universal transversal gate set |

These statements share examples but not proofs. BPT uses correctable-region
entropy and a geometric partition. It does not follow from the
Bravyi–König commutator argument, and neither theorem says that a surface
code is self-correcting.

## 10. Audit questions

**Q1. Why does distance first suggest only a \(\sqrt d\)-sized correctable
square, yet the proof obtains a \(d\)-sized square?**

**A.** Distance alone counts the square's area: fewer than \(d\) sites gives
side \(O(\sqrt d)\). Commuting locality changes the bottleneck from area to
boundary. The Growth Lemma says a correctable interior can keep expanding
until its width-\(w\) boundary collar has \(O(d)\) sites, which occurs at
side \(O(d/w)\).

**Q2. Where exactly is commutativity used?**

**A.** It makes the left and right interaction algebras on a boundary
commute. Their direct-sum tensor-product decomposition gives the
Disentangling Lemma and the Separated-Union Lemma. The final entropy
inequalities alone do not use commutativity.

**Q3. Why are two correctable checkerboards needed?**

**A.** One correctable region gives
\(k\leq S(B)+S(C)-S(A)\), which still contains the extensive difference
\(S(B)-S(A)\). Applying the same identity to \(B\) gives the opposite
difference; adding cancels both and leaves \(k\leq S(C)\).

**Q4. Why are the removed regions corner patches rather than corridors?**

**A.** Same-colored checkerboard tiles meet only at corners. Removing
bounded patches there separates equal colors. There are
\(O(n/\ell^2)\) corners, so the remainder has the \(1/\ell^2\) density
needed for \(1/d^2\). Width-\(w\) corridors would have density
\(O(w/\ell)\) and lose one power.

**Q5. Does a finite block with \(kd^2/n>1\) violate BPT?**

**A.** No. The constant in \(O(n)\) is not universally one, and a single
finite block cannot violate an asymptotic statement. To apply BPT to a
family, \(q\), the Euclidean interaction range, and the geometric
bounded-density constants must all remain fixed as \(n\) grows.

**Q6. Why does the theorem include non-Pauli commuting-projector codes but
exclude generic subsystem codes?**

**A.** Pauli algebra is not used. Pairwise commutativity of the defining
projectors is. Local subsystem gauge generators generally do not commute,
and their commuting stabilizers may be geometrically nonlocal, so the
boundary-algebra step does not automatically apply.

## 11. Source and citation audit

Primary source, fetch-verified on 2026-07-28:

- Sergey Bravyi, David Poulin, and Barbara Terhal, “Tradeoffs for reliable
  quantum information storage in 2D systems,”
  [arXiv:0909.5200](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.5200), submitted
  28 September 2009; [Physical Review Letters 104, 050503
  (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.050503).

Boundary-algebra source, also fetch-verified on 2026-07-28:

- Sergey Bravyi and Mikhail Vyalyi, “Commutative version of the \(k\)-local
  Hamiltonian problem and common eigenspace problem,”
  [arXiv:quant-ph/0308021](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0308021);
  *Quantum Information & Computation* 5, 187–215 (2005).

The precise hypotheses, erasure definition of distance, entropy identity,
Disentangling Lemma, Growth Lemma, separated-union argument, checkerboard
partition, quantum bound, classical contrast, and \(D\)-dimensional
generalization trace to the primary BPT source. This page expands the
boundary-algebra step, correctability criterion, entropy cancellation, and
constant-scale choices so that the cited paper supplies provenance rather
than a missing proof.

Atlas citation note: `atlas/surface/card.yaml` uses the bibkey
`bravyi2010tradeoffs`, while
`docs/lit/surface/surface-foundations.md` uses
`bravyipoulinterhal2010tradeoffs` for the same fetch-verified paper. T5
permits new files only, so this page records the mismatch instead of changing

# Knill–Laflamme conditions

title: Pauli operators as binary symplectic vectors
markdown:
# Pauli operators as binary symplectic vectors

## Essence

Ignore a Pauli operator's global phase and record, for each qubit, whether an
`X` component and a `Z` component are present. The operator becomes

\[
P \longleftrightarrow [x\mid z]\in \mathbb F_2^{2n},
\qquad
I=(0,0),\;X=(1,0),\;Z=(0,1),\;Y=(1,1).
\]

The order is fixed: all `x` bits in increasing qubit order, then all `z`
bits. There is no hidden phase field. This convention is the exact
`phase-free-x-then-z-bits-v1` interface used by the machine proof.

Two phase-free Paulis commute precisely when

\[
\langle[x\mid z],[x'\mid z']\rangle_s
=x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'=0\pmod 2.
\]

That formula is not a mnemonic. It counts, modulo two, the qubits where the
local factors anticommute.

## Why the parity is the whole commutation test

At one qubit, `X` anticommutes with `Z`; the same is true for the pairs
`X,Y` and `Y,Z`. In binary coordinates, the local indicator is

\[
x_i z'_i+z_i x'_i \pmod 2.
\]

Check the four possibilities for each operand's `(x_i,z_i)` pair: the
indicator is one exactly for the six ordered pairs of distinct nonidentity
Paulis that anticommute, and zero otherwise. Tensor factors on different
qubits commute past each other. Moving the entire left Pauli past the right
one therefore contributes one minus sign per locally anticommuting overlap.
The global sign is positive exactly when their number is even, which is the
vanishing symplectic sum above.

This derivation also explains why global phase is safely omitted here. A phase
multiplies the complete operator by a scalar, so it does not change which
local swaps contribute minus signs. Phase matters for representing the full
Pauli group; it does not change this commutation predicate.

## Three pictures of the same calculation

### Bit-string picture

For `XX` and `ZZ`, the serialized rows are

\[
[1,1\mid0,0],\qquad[0,0\mid1,1].
\]

Each qubit contributes one, so the sum is zero in \(\mathbb F_2\): the two
minus signs cancel and the operators commute. For `X_` and `Z_`, only the
first qubit contributes, so the sum is one and the operators anticommute.

These are the two frozen fixtures. Their expectations are recomputed by
`qeclib.pauli.Pauli.commutes` and by Lean rather than copied as claimed data.

### Crossing-count picture

Draw an `X` mark from the first operator and a `Z` mark from the second at each
shared qubit; draw the reverse `Z`–`X` marks as well. Every crossing means one
local anticommutation. The symplectic inner product is simply the parity of
those crossings. This picture makes the two terms \(x\cdot z'\) and
\(z\cdot x'\) visible.

### Matrix picture

With column vectors \(v=[x\mid z]^T\) and \(w=[x'\mid z']^T\), define

\[
\Lambda=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Then \(\langle v,w\rangle_s=v^T\Lambda w\). A collection of stabilizer rows
is mutually commuting exactly when its binary check matrix \(H\) satisfies
\(H\Lambda H^T=0\). The pairwise parity rule and the matrix criterion are the
same statement at different scales.

## What the Lean bridge proves

The bridge is deliberately small. It imports only
`QEC.Stabilizer.Foundations.BinarySymplectic.SymplecticInner` from the exact
pinned QECLean checkout and defines a total translation from any two Boolean
functions `x z : Fin n → Bool` to QECLean's phase-zero Pauli group element.

Its first theorem expands the QECLean symplectic sum term by term and proves
that it equals the Atlas sum above. Its second theorem rewrites QECLean's named
`commutes_iff_symplectic_inner_zero` theorem through that equality. Thus the
machine-checked chain is

\[
\text{Atlas bits}
\rightarrow\text{QECLean Pauli}
\rightarrow\text{QECLean symplectic product}
\rightarrow\text{commutation}.
\]

The proof then evaluates both frozen fixtures and prints every theorem's axiom
dependencies. Accepted output may use only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and
`Quot.sound`; `sorry`, `sorryAx`, `Lean.ofReduceBool`, and `native_decide` are
refused. The committed manifest is verified offline during `make verify`.
Re-running Lean itself is opt-in because it requires the exact pinned external
toolchain and dependency checkout.

The machine result has origin
`{kind: verified, method: v9-production-focused-qeclean-replay}`. Its resource
limits have origin
`{kind: bounded, method: human-owner-authorized-t139-v8-envelope-2026-08-15}`.

## What this proof does not claim

This bridge proves the representation and commutation seam only. It does not
formalize a stabilizer code, CSS construction, distance, decoder, threshold,
or any Atlas code instance. It also does not close the broader Lean Wanted
item. Those gaps stay explicit because a trustworthy narrow theorem is more
useful than an umbrella claim whose assumptions and trust boundary are hard to
audit.

## Litmus questions

- Given `[x|z]`, can you recover the local Pauli at every qubit without a phase
  convention left unspecified?
- Can you point to the two local anticommutations that make `XX` commute with
  `ZZ`?
- Can you explain why a single `X_`–`Z_` overlap changes the parity?
- Can you derive `HΛHᵀ=0` by applying the pairwise rule to every row pair?
- Can you state exactly where the checked bridge stops before making a claim
  about stabilizer codes or distance?
